## Wall types typically used in Sweden

Swedish residential construction (especially single-family homes) almost universally uses **timber frame construction** (*träregelstomme*), not masonry or concrete block, because:
- Timber is locally abundant and well-suited to the climate
- It performs well thermally when filled with mineral wool insulation
- It meets **BBR** (Boverkets byggregler) energy performance requirements more easily than solid masonry

The standard exterior wall build-up is a **layered composite wall**, typically:

| Layer (outside → inside) | Material | Typical thickness |
|---|---|---|
| Cladding | Wood panel (*träpanel*) or render | 22 mm |
| Air gap / ventilation | Battens (*läkt*) | 28 mm |
| Wind barrier | Wind-proof board (*vindskyddsskiva*) | 12 mm |
| Structural frame + insulation | Timber studs (*regel*) 45×195 or 45×220 mm, filled with mineral wool | 195–220 mm |
| Vapor barrier | Plastic membrane (*plastfolie*) | — |
| Installation layer | Horizontal battens for wiring/pipes, often with extra 45 mm mineral wool | 45 mm |
| Interior finish | Gypsum board (*gips*) | 13 mm |

This gives a total wall thickness around **345–370 mm**, achieving a U-value near **0.13–0.18 W/m²K**, which comfortably meets current BBR requirements for exterior walls in most Swedish climate zones.

## Example: building this composite in Archicad

1. Open **Wall Default Settings** → **Structure** → click the composite editor (pencil icon)
2. Create a new composite, name it something like `YW_Exterior_345_Timber`
3. Add layers top to bottom (from the composite editor's layer list), each with a **Function** tag and **Building Material**:
   - `Finish 1`: Wood cladding, 22 mm
   - `Air gap`: Air gap, 28 mm (use "Miscellaneous" function, hatch as air)
   - `Finish 2`: Wind barrier board, 12 mm
   - `Core`: Timber stud + mineral wool, 220 mm (this is the load-bearing "Core" — Archicad needs exactly one Core layer)
   - `Core 2` or `Other`: Installation layer, mineral wool, 45 mm
   - `Finish 3`: Vapor barrier (very thin, ~0.2 mm, or just noted as a separator without real thickness)
   - `Finish 4`: Gypsum board, 13 mm
4. Set the reference line to **Core** — this keeps your wall's dimension line anchored to the structural timber frame regardless of finish changes later
5. Assign this composite as your default exterior wall and draw

## Most common floor types in Sweden

For a single-family home like yours, there are two floor conditions to think about — the **ground floor** (touching the earth) and **intermediate floors** (between stories, e.g. ground to first floor).

**Ground floor — "platta på mark" (slab on grade)**
This is by far the most common ground-floor solution in new Swedish construction. A concrete slab poured directly on insulation, sitting on the ground:

| Layer (bottom → top) | Material | Typical thickness |
|---|---|---|
| Sub-base | Compacted gravel/crushed rock | 300+ mm |
| Insulation | EPS (cellplast) | 200–300 mm |
| Radon/moisture barrier | Plastic membrane | — |
| Structural slab | Reinforced concrete | 100 mm |
| Floor heating (optional) | Pipes cast in or on top | — |
| Screed/finish | Self-leveling screed + flooring | 50–80 mm |

This gives good thermal performance and avoids the moisture/mold problems that older **crawl space (krypgrund)** timber floors were prone to — crawl spaces are still used but less common in new builds now.

**Intermediate floor — timber joist floor (bjälklag)**
Between ground and first floor, timber joists are standard:

| Layer | Material | Typical size |
|---|---|---|
| Flooring | Wood/laminate | 14–22 mm |
| Subfloor | Chipboard/OSB | 22 mm |
| Joists + insulation | Timber joists (typically 45×220–270 mm) with mineral wool between, for sound/fire separation | 220–270 mm |
| Ceiling | Gypsum board, often on resilient sound bars | 13 mm |
